arc_intro:
FQ-203 — Deepak Menon (DevOps Lead)

I'm the new DevOps hire — first dedicated headcount for infrastructure monitoring at FoodQuick, which itself should tell you something about how this has been handled until now. Ravi's brought me in because the company keeps finding out about production issues from customer complaints on social media, not from anything internal.

Before I build anything new, I want a full picture of what's actually already being logged and monitored — and I have a feeling a good chunk of it has been quietly running up a bill nobody's looked at.

— Deepak

P.S. — Ravi mentioned you've done good work on the last three tickets. Good, I'd rather inherit a well-understood account than a mystery box.
arc_outro:
Deepak Menon (DevOps Lead)

Exactly the kind of thing I expected to find — years of logs nobody ever told CloudWatch to forget, quietly costing real money the whole time. Retention policies in place now, and Logs Insights is going to save real time going forward instead of manually scrolling through log streams.

One more thing you found while you were in there, though — that alarm. HighErrorRate-order-service has apparently been firing into an SNS topic with zero working subscribers for who knows how long. That's not a logging problem, that's a 'we thought we were watching and we weren't' problem, and it's exactly the kind of thing this whole ticket exists to fix. Let's keep an eye on that as we go.

— Deepak

tasks.question: What is a CloudWatch namespace, and what's it used for?
options: A) A namespace is a security boundary that prevents different AWS accounts from seeing each other's metrics, with no other purpose

B) A namespace is a logical container that groups related metrics together (e.g. AWS/EC2 for EC2 metrics, AWS/RDS for RDS metrics, or a custom namespace like FoodQuick/OrderService for application-specific metrics) — it's how CloudWatch organizes and separates different sources of metric data
C) A namespace is a billing construct with no relationship to how metrics are actually organized
D) Every AWS account can only have exactly one namespace, shared across all services

tasks.question: What's the relationship between a CloudWatch Logs GROUP and a log STREAM within it?
options: A) They're the same thing, just two different names used interchangeably

C) A log stream can belong to multiple log groups simultaneously
D) Log groups are created automatically only for RDS, never for any other AWS service

2.1TB of accumulated log data represents real, ongoing storage cost that's been silently accruing this whole time

The one correctly-configured group (RDS postgresql logs, 7-day retention) proves this isn't a universal account setting — someone deliberately configured that one correctly, while the others were simply never touched

tasks.scenario: While reviewing existing CloudWatch resources as part of this same audit, you notice an alarm called HighErrorRate-order-service, currently showing repeated ALARM state transitions in its history over the past several months.
tasks.error_shown:
$ aws cloudwatch describe-alarm-history --alarm-name HighErrorRate-order-service
[47 ALARM state transitions over the past 6 months]

$ aws sns get-topic-attributes --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:ap-south-1:xxxx:order-service-alerts
"SubscriptionsConfirmed": "0",
"SubscriptionsPending": "0"
(zero confirmed subscribers — the topic exists, the alarm fires into it correctly, but nothing and no one is actually listening)
tasks.diagnosis: This alarm has been correctly detecting real elevated error rates 47 times over 6 months and correctly notifying its configured SNS topic every time — but that topic has zero subscribers, confirmed or pending. Somewhere along the way, whoever used to be subscribed (likely an email subscription that was removed, or an employee who left without the subscription being transferred) stopped receiving these, and nobody set up a replacement. The monitoring technically worked; the notification path to an actual human was silently broken.
tasks.fix: This is a separate, ongoing finding — do not fix it in isolation as a quick patch. Flag it explicitly to Deepak as a real example of exactly the 'flying blind' pattern this whole ticket exists to address, and continue the broader monitoring audit with this open, to be addressed properly (likely in the alarms/SNS work coming up) rather than a rushed one-line fix.

cases.case_1: Application debug logs used only for occasional troubleshooting, no compliance relevance
cases.case_2: Logs related to authentication/access events, which might be needed if a security question arises weeks or months later
cases.case_3: Extremely high-volume, low-value debug logs from a noisy library that rarely helps diagnose anything
cases.case_4: Logs a specific regulatory requirement mandates keeping for at least 1 year

correct_answers.case_1: Short retention (30-90 days) — enough window for typical troubleshooting, no reason to pay for longer storage
correct_answers.case_2: Longer retention (e.g. 6-12 months), decided deliberately based on realistic investigation timelines, not left at the accidental default of 'forever'
correct_answers.case_3: Very short retention (7-14 days) or filtering at the source to reduce volume before it's even stored, since the log's actual debugging value is low relative to its volume
correct_answers.case_4: Retention matching or exceeding the specific regulatory minimum, documented with the requirement it satisfies — not guessed at

tasks.scenario: Deepak wants the real historical cost number for his first report to Ravi. The 2.1TB of accumulated logs cost roughly ₹2.60/GB-month to store, and had been accumulating for an average of about 20 months across the three affected log groups.
tasks.question: What's a reasonable estimate of the total historical cost of this oversight, and what's the go-forward savings from the new retention policies?
tasks.solution: Estimating the average accumulated volume over the 20-month period at roughly half the final 2.1TB (since it grew from zero) gives a rough historical cost estimate of approximately 1,050GB average × ₹2.60/GB-month × 20 months ≈ ₹54,600 in cumulative storage costs for log data with little to no remaining debugging value. Going forward, capping retention at 90/90/30 days instead of indefinite growth means storage cost stabilizes at a small, bounded amount per month instead of continuing to grow forever — a predictable, low ongoing cost instead of an ever-increasing one.
